transcript:
This is NPR News now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
G7 nations say they're planning to release 100 million barrels of oil from the reserves
to help ease rising fuel prices.
The release will begin immediately and continue over the next four months with diesel release
first.
President Trump has threatened to halt U.S. diesel exports unless Europe tapped its stockpiles.
White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett says Europe has substantial supplies available.
The Europeans have a different strategic reserve than the U.S. ours is crude and there's this
refined product and they have a massive, massive amount of refined product, especially diesel.
And so we think that they have room probably to help the world economy right now.
AAA says the price for a gallon of diesel now averages $6.35.
The price of jet fuel has hit record highs.
According to Airlines for America, the national average is about $4.39 per gallon.
President Trump's proposed triumphal arch in Washington, D.C. is getting closer to final
approval.
NPR's Rachel Treisman reports the project appears to be moving ahead despite public
opposition and an ongoing lawsuit.
A federal panel packed with Trump allies abruptly canceled the historic preservation review
process for his proposed arch last month, sidestepping one of the last remaining hurdles.
Concerned citizens this week joined veterans and Democratic lawmakers in Memorial Circle
to speak out against it.
John Gunderson is one of the Vietnam War veterans and retired foreign service members that has
sued the government to block the arch, which would tower over Arlington National Cemetery.
I hope people look at this, they look at it in a logical, nonpartisan way, it's a waste
of taxpayers' money, stop the arch.
Even if the arch does proceed, Democrats at the protest said they would fight to knock
it down.
Rachel Treisman, NPR News.
For nearly 50 years, the federal government has said segregating people with disabilities
and institutions is in most cases an act of discrimination, and NPR's Janaki Mehta reports
the Trump administration disagrees.
The Justice Department began shifting its position back in June, saying states didn't
have to integrate people with disabilities into their communities to follow the law.
It all culminated in a court case last week when a federal judge agreed to strip the concept,
even the word "integration," out of federal rules.
That doesn't change laws that protect integration, but experts like Jennifer Mathis, a disability
rights lawyer, say it sends a clear message.
It is a signal to states.
The federal government thinks they have permission to go institutionalize people.
Although the law hasn't changed, federal enforcement already has.
Janaki Mehta, NPR News.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
A new study shows eating with another person may help manage blood sugar.
Researchers gave two groups of participants the same amount of bread to eat, then measured
how their blood sugar rose and recovered, and NPR's Burlee McCoy reports.
In one group, the participants ate their bread alone, and the other, someone else was in
the room, and they found the social eaters recovered quicker.
That is, their blood sugar didn't spike as high, or came back down quicker, or both.
Lead author and behavioral neuroscientist Sheer Adzeel says this might be because humans
are social animals.
If my brain develops in a social context, my brain learns to regulate my glucose levels
in social proximity.
She says other people may be a social cue the brain uses to start processing sugar earlier,
for example, by releasing insulin, which helps regulate blood sugar.
The results appear in the journal Science Advances, Burlee McCoy, NPR News.
The FDA has closed its investigation into this year's cyclospora outbreak, the largest
on record in the U.S.
The agency says evidence strongly links iceberg lettuce to nearly 13,000 cases nationwide.
Inspectors found the parasite in a drainage ditch at a lettuce farm in Mexico and in a
wastewater tank at a processing facility.
Testigators still don't know exactly how the contamination occurred.
Taylor Farms, which distributed the lettuce, blames an independent grower and says it no
longer uses that supplier.
I'm Winsor Johnston, NPR News, in Washington.
